questions.problem:
Find the standard matrix that  represents  the  linear  transformation $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{2},$ where

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x-y+z \\ x-y-z\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We require a $2\times 3$ matrix $T$ such that

$$
T\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2x+(-1)y+1z \\ 1x+(-1)y+(-1)z\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2x-y+z \\ x-y-z\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the matrix which represents the linear transformation $T$ is
    

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the standard matrix that represents  the  linear  transformation $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{4},$ where

questions.worked_solution:
We require a $4\times 3$ matrix $T$ such that
    

$$
T\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}(-4)x+5y+(-1)z \\ 3x+(-2)y+7z \\ (-6)x+1y+0z \\ (-3)x+8y+0z\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that
    

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4 & 5 & -1 \\ 3 & -2 & 7 \\ -6 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 8 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4x-z+5y \\ 3x+7z-2y \\ -6x+y \\ 8y-3x\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the matrix which represents the linear transformation $T$ is
    

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4 & 5 & -1 \\ 3 & -2 & 7 \\ -6 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 8 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Given the vector $\,[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5x+3y \\ -2x+4y \\ 3x-y\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3y+5x \\ -2x+4y \\ -y+3x\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the linear transformation $T$ is given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3y+5x \\ (-2)x+4y \\ (-1)y+3x\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a+b+c=5+(-2)+(-1)=2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-8 & -5 \\ -3 & -6 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-8x-5y \\ -3x-6y \\ -4x+5y\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5y-8x \\ -3x-6y \\ 5y-4x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ is given by

Finally, $a-b=(-5)-(-4)=-1.$

Example: 
                    Finding the Image of a Vector Under a Linear Map
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the matrix $T$ and the vector $\mathbf{v}$ given below. If $T$ is the standard matrix of the linear transformation $\mathbf{T}:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2,$ find $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14136609/assets/46bb3e9777a3944eb6b2f458911571442f57a5fae2f7aed1bb924522c51cad4a.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the fact that $\,\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})=T\cdot \mathbf{v},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(v) & =T\cdot v \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.problem:
Similar to transformations in a vector space, we can define a transformation between two *different* vector spaces. For instance, consider the transformation that maps the vector 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]
$$

from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to the vector 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x+y \\ x-y \\ 2x+2y\end{aligned}]
$$

in $\mathbb{R}^3,$ which can be written as

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14136609/assets/ac48dfb4fa4df769cc32789336d9f76960bde087351adf44328c33ebb1c40545.svg)

The *standard matrix* of this transformation is 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14136609/assets/0a94602cefa1750e0833e75a9a1e368d5d4164703fc85319db56cbfc28512194.svg)

Recall that a transformation $\mathbf{T}: V \to W$ between two vector spaces $V$ and $W$ is *linear* if for any vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2\in V$ and any scalar $k\in\mathbb{R}$, the following conditions are satisfied:

- $\mathbf{T}(k\mathbf{v}_1) = k\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1)$

- $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1+\mathbf{v}_2) = \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1)+\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_2)$

It is easy to check that if a transformation can be represented as a matrix, then it is a linear transformation. Therefore, the transformation $\mathbf{S}$ is a linear transformation.

In general, if $V$ and $W$ are $n$-dimensional and $m$-dimensional vector spaces respectively, then the standard matrix of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}\!: V \!\rightarrow W$ is an $m\times n$ matrix $T$.

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
Similar to transformations in a vector space, we can define a transformation between two *different* vector spaces. For instance, consider the transformation that maps the vector 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]
$$

from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to the vector 

$$
[\begin{aligned}x+y \\ x-y \\ 2x+2y\end{aligned}]
$$

in $\mathbb{R}^3,$ which can be written as

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14136609/assets/ac48dfb4fa4df769cc32789336d9f76960bde087351adf44328c33ebb1c40545.svg)

The *standard matrix* of this transformation is 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14136609/assets/0a94602cefa1750e0833e75a9a1e368d5d4164703fc85319db56cbfc28512194.svg)

Recall that a transformation $\mathbf{T}: V \to W$ between two vector spaces $V$ and $W$ is *linear* if for any vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2\in V$ and any scalar $k\in\mathbb{R}$, the following conditions are satisfied:

- $\mathbf{T}(k\mathbf{v}_1) = k\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1)$

- $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1+\mathbf{v}_2) = \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1)+\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_2)$

It is easy to check that if a transformation can be represented as a matrix, then it is a linear transformation. Therefore, the transformation $\mathbf{S}$ is a linear transformation.

In general, if $V$ and $W$ are $n$-dimensional and $m$-dimensional vector spaces respectively, then the standard matrix of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}\!: V \!\rightarrow W$ is an $m\times n$ matrix $T$.
